items.title: Bitcoin drops below $63,000 as Trump's 15% tariff takes effect

featured_image.name: Trump tariffs live updates: Trump raises 'global' tariff to 15%; US to stop collecting duties deemed illegal

items.description:
Bitcoin tumbled more than 5% on Tuesday, sliding below $63,000 as a new round of global tariffs took effect and escalating tensions in the Middle East pushed investors further away from risk assets. The leading cryptocurrency fell to a low of $62,964.64, according to CNBC, as market participants engaged in what analysts described as broad "tactical de-risking."[1]

The drop coincided with the midnight implementation of President Donald Trump's 15% global import tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 — a statute never before invoked by a president. Trump signed the measure on February 20, initially setting the rate at 10%, before raising it to the statutory maximum of 15% the following day via a post on Truth Social. The move came just hours after the U.S. Supreme Court, in a 6-3 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, struck down the administration's previous tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.[2][3][4][5][6][7]

items.title: Oil prices near 7-month highs as U.S.-Iran talks loom

featured_image.name: Oil hovers below seven-month high as traders eye U.S.–Iran talks ...

items.description:
Oil prices hovered near seven-month highs on Tuesday as traders weighed the prospect of a new round of U.S.-Iran nuclear talks against an increasingly bellicose tone from President Donald Trump, who warned Tehran of a "very bad day" if negotiations fail.

Brent crude futures rose 0.8% to $72.08 a barrel in early Asian trade on Tuesday, nearing their highest level since late July, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude climbed 0.9% to $66.88 a barrel. Both benchmarks had touched their firmest levels in roughly seven months during Monday's session, with Brent reaching $72.50 and WTI hitting $67.28, before pulling back.[1][2][3]

items.title: Rival studies clash over fate of massive dying star WOH G64

featured_image.name: SALT solves stellar mystery: WOH G64 still alive as a red ...

items.description:
WOH G64, one of the most extreme stars ever observed, is at the center of a scientific debate over whether it is on a path toward imminent destruction or simply behaving strangely under the influence of a companion star.

A study published February 23 in Nature Astronomy by a team led by Gonzalo Muñoz-Sanchez concludes that WOH G64 has undergone a "dramatic transition" from a red supergiant to a yellow hypergiant, a rare and unstable phase that can precede a supernova explosion. The researchers analyzed more than three decades of photometric and spectroscopic data, finding that the star's effective temperature increased by more than 1,000 degrees Kelvin since roughly 2014. They describe WOH G64 as a "rare, massive symbiotic binary system" and propose that the transition could result from the partial ejection of its outer envelope or the winding down of a decades-long eruption.[1][2][3]

items.title: Explosion near Moscow train station kills police officer on Ukraine war anniversary

featured_image.name: Man kills police officer in Moscow train station blast

items.description:
An unidentified assailant detonated an explosive device beside a police patrol vehicle at Savyolovsky Station Square in central Moscow early Tuesday, killing himself and a traffic police officer and wounding two others, Russian authorities said. The blast came just minutes into February 24 — the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The attack occurred at approximately 00:05 Moscow time, according to Moscow's branch of the Interior Ministry, which said the man approached officers sitting inside a patrol car before the device went off. One officer was killed instantly, while two others were hospitalized.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Ukraine reconstruction costs hit $588B as war marks four years

featured_image.name: Russia hits power stations after Ukraine counter-offensive

items.description:
As Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year on February 24, 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the war "a stain on our collective consciousness" and renewed his demand for "an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire" as a first step toward lasting peace. In remarks to the Human Rights Council on Monday, Guterres noted that more than 15,000 civilians have been killed and declared: "It is more than past time to end the bloodshed".[1][2][3][4]

The anniversary comes days after the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ended without a breakthrough in Geneva, where negotiations on territorial control and security guarantees remain at an impasse.[5][6]

items.title: Russian oil exports top prewar levels despite four years of sanctions

featured_image.name: Russia's crude exports slump to the lowest in 11 months

items.description:
Four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the volume of Russian crude oil being shipped abroad remains above prewar levels, even as the revenue Moscow earns from those barrels has fallen sharply, according to new data published on the fourth anniversary of the conflict.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Finland-based think tank known as CREA, reported on Tuesday that Russian crude oil export volumes in the 12 months ending February 24, 2026, remained six percent above pre-invasion levels, totaling 215 million tonnes. Yet revenues from those crude exports dropped 18 percent year-on-year to 85.5 billion euros, as Russia has been forced to sell at steep discounts to attract buyers. Total fossil fuel export revenues fell to an estimated 193 billion euros for the period, down 27 percent from comparable pre-invasion levels.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: EU leaders visit Kyiv as Ukraine marks four years of war

featured_image.name: Ukraine marks four years since Russian invasion - Yahoo

items.description:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2026 — exactly four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion — Ukraine entered a fifth year of fighting with no end in sight, as its people continue to endure daily bombardment, displacement, and an energy crisis that has left millions shivering through one of the harshest winters in recent memory.

Senior European Union leaders traveled to Kyiv to mark the occasion. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa attended an official memorial ceremony, visited energy infrastructure damaged by Russian missile strikes, and held a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Coalition of the Willing, a group of 35 countries convened by British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron, held a videoconference reaffirming support for Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte participated in a separate ceremony at NATO headquarters in Brussels.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Waterloo researchers turn plastic waste into vinegar using sunlight

featured_image.name: Iron catalyst turns plastic waste into vinegar using sunlight

items.description: Researchers at the University of Waterloo have developed a sunlight-driven process that converts plastic waste, including microplastics, into acetic acid — the main component of vinegar — using a catalyst inspired by the way fungi break down organic matter in nature.

items.title: 2026 is deadliest start to a year for Mediterranean migrants, UN says

featured_image.name: Migrant boat docks in Crete after dramatic rescue

items.description:
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration announced Monday that at least 606 migrants have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean Sea since the beginning of 2026, making it the deadliest start to a year since the agency began tracking such data in 2014.[1][2][3]

The grim milestone came as search operations continued off the Greek island of Crete, where a vessel carrying roughly 50 people capsized on Saturday approximately 20 nautical miles south of the port of Kali Limenes. Twenty people were rescued, including four minors, and the bodies of three men and one woman were recovered, according to the Associated Press. About 30 others remain unaccounted for.[4][1]

items.title: Slovakia cuts emergency power to Ukraine over oil dispute

featured_image.name: Slovakia threatens to cut electricity to Ukraine over Russian oil spat

items.description:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Monday ordered the state-run Slovak Electricity Transmission System (SEPS) to suspend emergency electricity supplies to Ukraine, making good on a two-day ultimatum that expired after Kyiv did not restore oil flows through the Druzhba pipeline.

"As of today, if the Ukrainian side contacts Slovakia seeking help to stabilize the Ukrainian energy grid, such assistance will be denied," Fico said in a video posted to Facebook. He said the measure would be reversed "immediately after the resumption of oil transit to Slovakia" and warned that further "reciprocal measures" could follow, including reconsidering Slovakia's previously supportive stance on Ukraine's EU membership.[1][2][3]

items.title: Venezuela frees nearly 2,200 under new amnesty law

featured_image.name: Venezuela has released nearly 2,200 people under new amnesty ...

items.description:
Nearly 2,200 people have been released from Venezuelan jails since a new amnesty law took effect on Friday, lawmaker Jorge Arreaza announced on Monday. Arreaza, who leads the commission set up to monitor the law's implementation, disclosed the figure as emotional scenes of family reunions played out at facilities including El Rodeo prison east of Caracas.[1][2][3][4]

The releases mark a rapid escalation from the weekend, when National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez said 1,557 amnesty requests were being processed "immediately" and that "hundreds of releases" were already underway. The law, unanimously approved by Venezuela's ruling party-dominated National Assembly on February 19, offers amnesty for crimes linked to political protests and confrontations dating from 1999 to 2026.[5][6][7][8]

items.title: France bars US envoy Kushner from government access

featured_image.name: France to summon Ambassador Charles Kushner over U.S. ...

items.description:
France on Monday blocked US Ambassador Charles Kushner from direct access to government ministers after he failed to appear at a scheduled evening summons at the Quai d'Orsay, the headquarters of the Foreign Affairs Ministry. According to a source cited by AFP, Kushner sent a senior embassy official in his place, citing personal obligations.[1]

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot had called Kushner in to explain the Trump administration's remarks about the killing of Quentin Deranque, a 23-year-old far-right activist who died on February 14 from brain injuries sustained two days earlier during clashes between far-right and far-left groups in Lyon. In response to Kushner's absence, Barrot moved to curtail the ambassador's privileges, acting "in light of this apparent misunderstanding of the basic expectations of the mission of an ambassador, who has the honor of representing his country," according to the foreign ministry.[2][3][4][5]

items.title: Study finds proto-writing on Stone Age artifacts in Germany from 40,000 years ago

featured_image.name: Stone Age symbols may push back the earliest form of writing

items.description:
More than 40,000 years ago, early humans living in what is now southern Germany were carving structured sequences of symbols onto ivory tools and figurines — marks that a new study argues represent the earliest known precursors to writing, predating the emergence of proto-cuneiform script in Mesopotamia by more than 30,000 years.

The findings, set to be published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, come from a collaboration between linguist Christian Bentz at Saarland University and archaeologist Ewa Dutkiewicz at the Museum of Prehistory and Early History in Berlin. Using computational methods drawn from information theory and quantitative linguistics, the team analyzed more than 3,000 individual marks found on 260 Aurignacian-era artifacts unearthed in the Swabian Jura region of southwestern Germany.[1][2]

items.title: Anthropic says Chinese AI labs used 24,000 fake accounts to copy Claude

featured_image.name: Top AI firm alleges Chinese labs used 24K fake accounts to siphon US tech

items.description:
Anthropic alleged on Monday that three Chinese artificial intelligence companies — DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and MiniMax — used roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts to extract capabilities from its Claude chatbot in a coordinated effort the company described as industrial-scale distillation, according to a blog post and a report first obtained by Fox News Digital.[1][2]

The three firms prompted Claude more than 16 million times, siphoning outputs to train and improve their own AI systems, Anthropic said. The scale of each company's activity varied: MiniMax accounted for more than 13 million interactions, Moonshot AI for more than 3.4 million, and DeepSeek for 150,000, according to The Wall Street Journal.[3]

items.title: Trump's top general warns of major risks in Iran strike

featured_image.name: Trump's top general warns of Iran strike risks

items.description:
As President Trump weighs whether to launch a military campaign against Iran, his top military adviser is delivering a sober message: this would not be another Venezuela.

Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has been cautioning Trump and senior officials about the substantial risks of a military operation against Iran, including the prospect of U.S. casualties, strained military resources, and a prolonged regional conflict, according to an Axios report citing sources familiar with the internal deliberations. One source described Caine as a "reluctant warrior" on Iran, a contrast to the full-throated support he gave for the January operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.[1][2]

During a Situation Room meeting on Wednesday, Trump pressed Caine and CIA Director John Ratcliffe for assessments of the broader Iran strategy, according to the New York Times. Where Caine had expressed a "high probability of success" before the Maduro operation, he has been unable to offer Trump similar reassurances on Iran, owing to the far greater complexities involved.[3][1]

items.title: Peter Mandelson arrested in probe tied to Epstein

featured_image.name: UK police launch investigation into ex-envoy Mandelson over Epstein ties

items.description:
Peter Mandelson, the former UK ambassador to the United States, was arrested on Monday at his home in Camden, north London, on suspicion of misconduct in public office as part of a Metropolitan Police investigation into his ties to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.[1][2][3]

"Officers have arrested a 72-year-old man on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He was arrested at an address in Camden on Monday, 23 February and has been taken to a London police station for interview," the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. The arrest followed the execution of search warrants at two addresses in the Wiltshire and Camden areas.[3][4][1]

items.title: Ukraine marks 4 years of war with nearly 2 million casualties and no peace deal

featured_image.name: Ukraine updates: Kyiv marks 2 years since Russian invasion

items.description: As Ukraine prepares to mark the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion on February 24, the war has exacted an almost incomprehensible human cost: nearly 1.8 million military casualties on both sides, more than 15,000 civilians killed, and millions displaced from their homes, with no peace agreement in sight.

items.title: Congo Basin lakes venting thousands-year-old carbon, study finds

featured_image.name: Peatland lakes in the Congo Basin release carbon that is ...

items.description: Two large blackwater lakes in the heart of the Congo Basin are acting as "chimneys," venting carbon that has been locked in surrounding peatlands for thousands of years, according to a study published Saturday in Nature Geoscience. The finding upends the long-held assumption that carbon stored in pristine tropical peat remains safely buried, and raises fresh concerns about the stability of one of the planet's most important carbon reservoirs.[1]

items.title: Russian small businesses buckle under wartime tax hikes as Ukraine invasion hits four years

featured_image.name: From bakeries to beauty shops, Russian businesses are feeling the ...

items.description:
As Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine marks its fourth anniversary, the economic toll of the war is reaching deeper into Russia's domestic economy. Small business owners across the country — from bakeries to beauty salons — report rising costs, collapsing demand, and a tax burden that has in some cases multiplied overnight, the result of sweeping fiscal reforms that took effect on January 1, 2026.

The reforms, signed into law by President Vladimir Putin in late November 2025, raised Russia's base value-added tax rate from 20% to 22% and drastically lowered the revenue threshold at which businesses must begin paying it — from 60 million rubles (approximately $783,000) to 20 million rubles ($261,000), with further reductions to 10 million rubles ($130,500) planned by 2028. The measures are designed to close a widening budget gap driven by soaring military expenditures and falling oil revenues.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Oil prices drop as US-Iran nuclear talks resume, tariffs rise

featured_image.name: Oil analysts say there is a supply glut — why that hasn't translated to lower prices this year

items.description:
Oil prices fell about 1% on Monday as the prospect of a third round of US-Iran nuclear talks eased fears of a military confrontation in the Middle East, while President Donald Trump's move to raise tariffs on all US imports to 15% added fresh uncertainty about the global economy.

Brent crude futures declined to around $71 a barrel, and US West Texas Intermediate futures dropped to roughly $66 a barrel, retreating after both benchmarks had surged more than 5% in the prior week on fears of a US-Iran military escalation.[1][2]
